Reference: Abadie (2005)

Model Setting

The paper relaxes the identifying assumption of the conventional difference-in-differences (DID) estimator, namely that in the absence of treatment the average outcomes of treated and controls would have followed parallel paths. Parallel paths are implausible when pre-treatment characteristics that drive outcome dynamics are unbalanced between the two groups, for instance when selection into a training programme responds to a transitory dip in pre-programme earnings (Ashenfelter's dip). The paper instead assumes conditional parallel trends: paths are parallel only among individuals with the same observed covariates. Under this assumption it shows that the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) equals a simple weighted average of outcome changes, with weights that depend only on the propensity score, so the propensity score is the only function to be estimated in a first step. This suggests a two-step estimator in the spirit of the Horvitz and Thompson (1952) statistic, rather than the matching estimator of Heckman, Ichimura and Todd (1997), which needs nonparametric weights from local linear regression.

The framework has three further features. It works with repeated cross sections as well as panels, so it has the same data requirements as the conventional DID estimator. It delivers parsimonious parametric (least-squares) approximations to how the ATT varies with selected covariates, while identification stays fully nonparametric: covariates enter the propensity score nonparametrically, and a parametric function is only a summary of the conditional ATT. It also accommodates selection on observables and multilevel treatments. The paper derives root-nnn asymptotic normality and consistent variance estimators for the two-step estimator when the propensity score is estimated by power series and when it is estimated by parametric maximum likelihood (logit, probit or linear probability). The article is purely methodological. It has no empirical application and reports no estimates. The motivating examples are the training-programme literature, minimum wages (Card and Krueger 1994), immigration (Card 1990), disability benefits (Meyer, Viscusi and Durbin 1995) and anti-takeover laws (Garvey and Hanka 1999).

The Conventional DID Model

P(D(i,1)=1∣υ(i,t))=P(D(i,1)=1),t=0,1(2)P(D(i,1)=1\mid\upsilon(i,t))=P(D(i,1)=1),\qquad t=0,1 \tag{2}P(D(i,1)=1∣υ(i,t))=P(D(i,1)=1),t=0,1(2)

The model implies that υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)\upsilon(i,1)-\upsilon(i,0)υ(i,1)−υ(i,0) is mean independent of treatment, so the untreated outcome changes are the same on average for both groups. This fails under the selection rule of Ashenfelter and Card (1985):

D(i,1)={1if Y(i,1−κ)+u(i)<Yˉ0otherwise(5)D(i,1)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }Y(i,1-\kappa)+u(i)<\bar{Y}\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} \tag{5}D(i,1)={10​if Y(i,1−κ)+u(i)<Yˉotherwise​(5)

Potential Outcomes and Conditional Parallel Trends

Y0(i,t)Y^0(i,t)Y0(i,t) and Y1(i,t)Y^1(i,t)Y1(i,t) are the potential outcomes without and with treatment (Rubin 1974; Heckman 1990). Dropping iii and writing D=D(i,1)D=D(i,1)D=D(i,1), treatment is only administered after t=0t=0t=0, so the observed outcomes are Y(0)=Y0(0)Y(0)=Y^0(0)Y(0)=Y0(0) and Y(1)=Y0(1)⋅(1−D)+Y1(1)⋅DY(1)=Y^0(1)\cdot(1-D)+Y^1(1)\cdot DY(1)=Y0(1)⋅(1−D)+Y1(1)⋅D. The targets are the ATT E[Y1(1)−Y0(1)∣D=1]E[Y^1(1)-Y^0(1)\mid D=1]E[Y1(1)−Y0(1)∣D=1] and its conditional version E[Y1(1)−Y0(1)∣X,D=1]E[Y^1(1)-Y^0(1)\mid X,D=1]E[Y1(1)−Y0(1)∣X,D=1], where XXX is a vector of covariates predetermined at t=0t=0t=0. The central restriction is:

Assumption 3.1 (conditional parallel trends).

E[Y0(1)−Y0(0)∣X,D=1]=E[Y0(1)−Y0(0)∣X,D=0](7)E[Y^0(1)-Y^0(0)\mid X,D=1]=E[Y^0(1)-Y^0(0)\mid X,D=0] \tag{7}E[Y0(1)−Y0(0)∣X,D=1]=E[Y0(1)−Y0(0)∣X,D=0](7)

Levels of untreated outcomes may differ arbitrarily between groups, and so may the distributions of unobservables, as long as the effect of unobservables on the outcome does not vary over time on average. When in addition E[Y0(0)∣X,D=1]=E[Y0(0)∣X,D=0]E[Y^0(0)\mid X,D=1]=E[Y^0(0)\mid X,D=0]E[Y0(0)∣X,D=1]=E[Y0(0)∣X,D=0], the assumption collapses to selection on observables, and Ashenfelter's dip is such a case. Following Heckman et al. (1997), Assumption 3.1 gives the conditional ATT as a conditional DID:

E[Y1(1)−Y0(1)∣X,D=1]={E[Y(1)∣X,D=1]−E[Y(1)∣X,D=0]}−{E[Y(0)∣X,D=1]−E[Y(0)∣X,D=0]}(8)\begin{aligned} E[Y^1(1)-Y^0(1)\mid X,D=1]&=\left\{E[Y(1)\mid X,D=1]-E[Y(1)\mid X,D=0]\right\}\\ &\quad-\left\{E[Y(0)\mid X,D=1]-E[Y(0)\mid X,D=0]\right\} \end{aligned} \tag{8}E[Y1(1)−Y0(1)∣X,D=1]​={E[Y(1)∣X,D=1]−E[Y(1)∣X,D=0]}−{E[Y(0)∣X,D=1]−E[Y(0)∣X,D=0]}​(8)

Estimating the four conditional expectations nonparametrically suffers from the curse of dimensionality, the result is hard to display when XXX has more than two dimensions, and summarizing it still requires integrating over the covariate distribution of the treated. Assumption 3.1 identifies E[Y0(1)∣X,D=1]E[Y^0(1)\mid X,D=1]E[Y0(1)∣X,D=1] but leaves E[Y1(1)∣X,D=0]E[Y^1(1)\mid X,D=0]E[Y1(1)∣X,D=0] unrestricted, so it does not identify the average effect conditional on XXX alone. The overlap condition is:

Assumption 3.2 (overlap). P(D=1)>0P(D=1)>0P(D=1)>0 and, with probability one, P(D=1∣X)<1P(D=1\mid X)<1P(D=1∣X)<1.

It requires some treated individuals and, at every covariate value, some controls, so the support of the propensity score among the treated is contained in its support among the untreated.

Treated changes get weight 1/P(D=1)1/P(D=1)1/P(D=1), and control changes get the negative weight −P(D=1∣X)/{P(D=0∣X)P(D=1)}-P(D=1\mid X)/\{P(D=0\mid X)P(D=1)\}−P(D=1∣X)/{P(D=0∣X)P(D=1)}. The scheme weights down control changes at covariate values over-represented among controls (low P(D=1∣X)/P(D=0∣X)P(D=1\mid X)/P(D=0\mid X)P(D=1∣X)/P(D=0∣X)) and weights up those at under-represented values, imposing the covariate distribution of the treated on the controls. The same balancing logic underlies propensity-score matching (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983). The two-step method is: (i) estimate P(D=1∣X)P(D=1\mid X)P(D=1∣X) and compute fitted values; (ii) plug them into the sample analogue of the last expression. Relative to the conditional DID formula, the first step uses all four (or both) groups of observations to estimate one function, and with too few observations for nonparametric estimation, parametric restrictions on the propensity score leave the conditional ATT itself unrestricted.

Repeated Cross Sections

With repeated cross sections, treatment status must be known for individuals in the pre-treatment sample, and covariates must be observed in the post-treatment sample. These are the requirements of conventional DID with covariates, as in Card (1990, 1992), Eissa and Liebman (1996), Acemoglu and Angrist (2001) and Finkelstein (2002). The pooled sample records Z=(Y,D,T,X)Z=(Y,D,T,X)Z=(Y,D,T,X), where T=1T=1T=1 for post-treatment observations.

Assumption 3.3. Conditional on T=0T=0T=0 the data are i.i.d. from (Y(0),D,X)(Y(0),D,X)(Y(0),D,X), and conditional on T=1T=1T=1 they are i.i.d. from (Y(1),D,X)(Y(1),D,X)(Y(1),D,X).

Takeaways

  • Identification: under conditional parallel trends and overlap, the ATT is a propensity-score-weighted mean of outcome changes (panel) or of time-reweighted outcome levels (repeated cross sections). No outcome regression is needed, and unobservables may differ between groups as long as their effect is time invariant on average.

  • Heterogeneity: the conditional ATT can be summarized by any parametric family g(Xk;θ)g(X_k;\theta)g(Xk​;θ) through a weighted regression of the transformed outcome. The weight P(D=1∣X)P(D=1\mid X)P(D=1∣X) makes the fit target the treated population, and misspecification of ggg affects only the quality of the summary, not identification.

  • Inference: the two-step estimator is root-nnn normal with either a series or a parametric first step. In both cases the variance must include a first-step correction, computed by a plug-in sandwich formula.

  • Practical caveats: the weights 1/(1−π0)1/(1-\pi_0)1/(1−π0​) explode when the propensity score approaches one, which is why overlap and the bound away from one in Assumptions 4.1 and 4.2 matter. In repeated cross sections, the variable that determines treatment status must be excluded from XXX, or the support condition fails.

References

  • Abadie, Alberto. 2005. “Semiparametric Difference-in-Differences Estimators.” The Review of Economic Studies, 72(1): 1–19.

This is the components of variance model of Ashenfelter and Card (1985) that underlies the conventional DID estimator. The outcome of individual iii in period t∈{0,1}t\in\{0,1\}t∈{0,1} is the sum of four pieces. δ(t)\delta(t)δ(t) is a period effect common to everybody (aggregate business cycle, inflation); α\alphaα is a constant treatment effect, switched on by D(i,t)D(i,t)D(i,t), which equals one only in the post period for the treated, since D(i,0)=0D(i,0)=0D(i,0)=0 for all iii; η(i)\eta(i)η(i) is a permanent individual effect (ability, location) whose distribution may differ arbitrarily between treated and controls; and υ(i,t)\upsilon(i,t)υ(i,t) is a transitory shock with mean zero in each period that may be serially correlated.

The form is restrictive in two ways that the paper later relaxes. First, the effect α\alphaα is homogeneous, so there is no notion of a conditional ATT. Second, the only source of group differences in untreated outcome dynamics is the shock υ\upsilonυ; the permanent component η(i)\eta(i)η(i) cancels in any time difference,

Y(i,1)−Y(i,0)=δ(1)−δ(0)+α⋅D(i,1)+υ(i,1)−υ(i,0).Y(i,1)-Y(i,0)=\delta(1)-\delta(0)+\alpha\cdot D(i,1)+\upsilon(i,1)-\upsilon(i,0).Y(i,1)−Y(i,0)=δ(1)−δ(0)+α⋅D(i,1)+υ(i,1)−υ(i,0).

Hence whether DID works depends only on how selection relates to υ\upsilonυ, which is what equation (2) restricts. Equations (3) and (4) are rewrites of this model under that restriction, and equation (5) gives a selection rule under which it fails.

This is the identifying condition of conventional DID: the probability of being treated does not depend on the transitory shock in either period. Because D(i,1)D(i,1)D(i,1) is binary, a conditional probability P(D(i,1)=1∣υ(i,t))P(D(i,1)=1\mid\upsilon(i,t))P(D(i,1)=1∣υ(i,t)) that does not vary with υ(i,t)\upsilon(i,t)υ(i,t) is the same as independence of D(i,1)D(i,1)D(i,1) and υ(i,t)\upsilon(i,t)υ(i,t), and therefore

E[υ(i,t)∣D(i,1)]=E[υ(i,t)]=0,t=0,1.E[\upsilon(i,t)\mid D(i,1)]=E[\upsilon(i,t)]=0,\qquad t=0,1.E[υ(i,t)∣D(i,1)]=E[υ(i,t)]=0,t=0,1.

What is allowed is just as important as what is ruled out: selection may depend in any way on the permanent effect η(i)\eta(i)η(i), so treated and controls can have different outcome levels. What is ruled out is selection on temporary outcome fluctuations, for example enrolling in training after an unusually bad year. The condition is sufficient, not necessary: DID only needs E[υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)∣D(i,1)]E[\upsilon(i,1)-\upsilon(i,0)\mid D(i,1)]E[υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)∣D(i,1)] to be constant, but the paper states the stronger version because it is what makes all regressors in equation (3) uncorrelated with the error. Equation (5) is a model in which this condition fails because serially correlated shocks drive participation, and Assumption 3.1, equation (7), is its conditional, potential-outcome generalization.

Start from equation (1). Since t∈{0,1}t\in\{0,1\}t∈{0,1}, the time effect can be written as an intercept plus a slope:

δ(t)=δ(0)+{δ(1)−δ(0)}⋅t=δ(0)+δ⋅t.\delta(t)=\delta(0)+\{\delta(1)-\delta(0)\}\cdot t=\delta(0)+\delta\cdot t.δ(t)=δ(0)+{δ(1)−δ(0)}⋅t=δ(0)+δ⋅t.

Add and subtract the conditional mean of the individual effect given treatment status. Because D(i,1)D(i,1)D(i,1) is binary, this conditional mean is linear in D(i,1)D(i,1)D(i,1):

E[η(i)∣D(i,1)]=E[η(i)∣D(i,1)=0]+τ⋅D(i,1),τ=E[η(i)∣D(i,1)=1]−E[η(i)∣D(i,1)=0].E[\eta(i)\mid D(i,1)]=E[\eta(i)\mid D(i,1)=0]+\tau\cdot D(i,1),\qquad \tau=E[\eta(i)\mid D(i,1)=1]-E[\eta(i)\mid D(i,1)=0].E[η(i)∣D(i,1)]=E[η(i)∣D(i,1)=0]+τ⋅D(i,1),τ=E[η(i)∣D(i,1)=1]−E[η(i)∣D(i,1)=0].

E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=1]=μ+τ+δ+α,E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=0]=μ+δ,E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=1]=μ+τ,E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=0]=μ.\begin{aligned} E[Y(i,1)\mid D(i,1)=1]&=\mu+\tau+\delta+\alpha, & E[Y(i,1)\mid D(i,1)=0]&=\mu+\delta,\\ E[Y(i,0)\mid D(i,1)=1]&=\mu+\tau, & E[Y(i,0)\mid D(i,1)=0]&=\mu. \end{aligned}E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=1]E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=1]​=μ+τ+δ+α,=μ+τ,​E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=0]E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=0]​=μ+δ,=μ.​

The post-period difference between groups is

E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=1]−E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=0]=τ+α,E[Y(i,1)\mid D(i,1)=1]-E[Y(i,1)\mid D(i,1)=0]=\tau+\alpha,E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=1]−E[Y(i,1)∣D(i,1)=0]=τ+α,

which mixes the permanent level gap τ\tauτ with the effect. The pre-period difference is

E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=1]−E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=0]=τ.E[Y(i,0)\mid D(i,1)=1]-E[Y(i,0)\mid D(i,1)=0]=\tau.E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=1]−E[Y(i,0)∣D(i,1)=0]=τ.

Subtracting the second from the first removes τ\tauτ and leaves α\alphaα, which is equation (4). Equivalently, differencing over time first gives δ+α\delta+\alphaδ+α for the treated and δ\deltaδ for the controls, and the second difference again yields α\alphaα. In a panel this equals the slope of a regression of Y(i,1)−Y(i,0)Y(i,1)-Y(i,0)Y(i,1)−Y(i,0) on a constant and D(i,1)D(i,1)D(i,1), because with a binary regressor the OLS slope is the difference in group means of the dependent variable.

This is the selection rule of Ashenfelter and Card (1985), used to show how conventional DID breaks down. An individual enrolls in the programme in period 111 when an earlier outcome, κ\kappaκ periods before the programme (so in period 1−κ≤01-\kappa\le 01−κ≤0), plus an idiosyncratic taste shock u(i)u(i)u(i) falls below a threshold Yˉ\bar{Y}Yˉ. With earnings as the outcome, people with low past earnings, for example after a layoff, are more likely to enter training.

Why equation (2) fails: by equation (1), Y(i,1−κ)Y(i,1-\kappa)Y(i,1−κ) contains the transitory shock υ(i,1−κ)\upsilon(i,1-\kappa)υ(i,1−κ). If υ\upsilonυ is serially correlated, a low υ(i,1−κ)\upsilon(i,1-\kappa)υ(i,1−κ) predicts low υ(i,0)\upsilon(i,0)υ(i,0), and with mean reversion the treated tend to have υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)>0\upsilon(i,1)-\upsilon(i,0)>0υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)>0 even without treatment. Hence

E[υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)∣D(i,1)=1]≠E[υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)∣D(i,1)=0],E[\upsilon(i,1)-\upsilon(i,0)\mid D(i,1)=1]\neq E[\upsilon(i,1)-\upsilon(i,0)\mid D(i,1)=0],E[υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)∣D(i,1)=1]=E[υ(i,1)−υ(i,0)∣D(i,1)=0],

and equation (4) attributes this mechanical recovery (Ashenfelter's dip) to the programme. The key observation is that D(i,1)D(i,1)D(i,1) depends on the shocks only through X(i)=Y(i,1−κ)X(i)=Y(i,1-\kappa)X(i)=Y(i,1−κ) and on u(i)u(i)u(i), which is independent of everything else. Conditional on X(i)X(i)X(i), selection is independent of the shocks, so DID is valid within cells of X(i)X(i)X(i). This motivates the conditional parallel trends condition in equation (7) with XXX including the pre-programme outcome.

The first line is the conventional linear fix: the covariates enter additively with period-specific coefficients π(t)\pi(t)π(t), which allows the covariates to shift outcome trends. It is a specification, not a result. The second line follows by writing the first line at t=1t=1t=1 and t=0t=0t=0 and subtracting. Use D(i,0)=0D(i,0)=0D(i,0)=0, so α⋅D(i,0)=0\alpha\cdot D(i,0)=0α⋅D(i,0)=0, and D(i,1)D(i,1)D(i,1) on both lines for the group term:

Y(i,1)=μ+X(i)′π(1)+τ⋅D(i,1)+δ+α⋅D(i,1)+ε(i,1),Y(i,0)=μ+X(i)′π(0)+τ⋅D(i,1)+ε(i,0).\begin{aligned} Y(i,1)&=\mu+X(i)'\pi(1)+\tau\cdot D(i,1)+\delta+\alpha\cdot D(i,1)+\varepsilon(i,1),\\ Y(i,0)&=\mu+X(i)'\pi(0)+\tau\cdot D(i,1)+\varepsilon(i,0). \end{aligned}Y(i,1)Y(i,0)​=μ+X(i)′π(1)+τ⋅D(i,1)+δ+α⋅D(i,1)+ε(i,1),=μ+X(i)′π(0)+τ⋅D(i,1)+ε(i,0).​

Subtracting, μ\muμ and the permanent group gap τ⋅D(i,1)\tau\cdot D(i,1)τ⋅D(i,1) cancel, and the covariate terms combine into X(i)′{π(1)−π(0)}=X(i)′πX(i)'\{\pi(1)-\pi(0)\}=X(i)'\piX(i)′{π(1)−π(0)}=X(i)′π:

Y(i,1)−Y(i,0)=δ+X(i)′π+α⋅D(i,1)+(ε(i,1)−ε(i,0)).Y(i,1)-Y(i,0)=\delta+X(i)'\pi+\alpha\cdot D(i,1)+(\varepsilon(i,1)-\varepsilon(i,0)).Y(i,1)−Y(i,0)=δ+X(i)′π+α⋅D(i,1)+(ε(i,1)−ε(i,0)).

Only the change in the coefficients is identified from a panel. The specification is restrictive in two ways that the semiparametric approach removes: the effect of X(i)X(i)X(i) on the trend is linear, and the treatment effect α\alphaα does not vary with X(i)X(i)X(i). If effects are heterogeneous and the treated have a different covariate distribution, OLS estimates of α\alphaα give a variance-weighted average of cell effects rather than the ATT.

Assumption 3.1, conditional parallel trends, is the identifying restriction of the paper. Among individuals with the same predetermined covariates XXX, the average change of the untreated potential outcome from period 000 to period 111 would have been the same for the treated (D=1D=1D=1) and the controls (D=0D=0D=0). It compares changes, not levels: E[Y0(0)∣X,D=1]E[Y^0(0)\mid X,D=1]E[Y0(0)∣X,D=1] and E[Y0(0)∣X,D=0]E[Y^0(0)\mid X,D=0]E[Y0(0)∣X,D=0] may differ arbitrarily, so selection on unobserved permanent characteristics is allowed.

The restriction relaxes the unconditional parallel trends condition in two ways. It only needs to hold within covariate cells, so differences in the covariate distribution that affect outcome dynamics, such as the pre-programme earnings in equation (5), are allowed. It is also stated in terms of potential outcomes, so it allows treatment effects that vary with XXX and across individuals. Two special cases: with XXX empty it reduces to the standard DID assumption behind equation (4); and if, in addition, pre-treatment levels are equal given XXX, it becomes selection on observables, equation (18). The assumption only restricts Y0Y^0Y0, so it identifies the effect on the treated (it pins down the counterfactual E[Y0(1)∣X,D=1]E[Y^0(1)\mid X,D=1]E[Y0(1)∣X,D=1]) but says nothing about E[Y1(1)∣X,D=0]E[Y^1(1)\mid X,D=0]E[Y1(1)∣X,D=0]. It is used in equations (8), (9) and (15). It is untestable without more periods; with several pre-periods, parallel pre-trends conditional on XXX are a common check.

Use the observation rule Y(0)=Y0(0)Y(0)=Y^0(0)Y(0)=Y0(0) (nobody is treated at t=0t=0t=0) and Y(1)=Y0(1)(1−D)+Y1(1)DY(1)=Y^0(1)(1-D)+Y^1(1)DY(1)=Y0(1)(1−D)+Y1(1)D. Within each group, the observed outcomes are the relevant potential outcomes:

This describes how a pooled pair of repeated cross sections is generated. Each observation in the pooled sample carries a time indicator TTT: with probability λ\lambdaλ it comes from the post-treatment survey (T=1T=1T=1), in which we see (Y(1),D,X)(Y(1),D,X)(Y(1),D,X), and with probability 1−λ1-\lambda1−λ from the pre-treatment survey (T=0T=0T=0), in which we see (Y(0),D,X)(Y(0),D,X)(Y(0),D,X). The observed YYY is Y(1)Y(1)Y(1) or Y(0)Y(0)Y(0) depending on TTT. The probabilities P(⋅)P(\cdot)P(⋅) on the right refer to the underlying population, which is the same in both periods; PMP_MPM​ is the mixture. In practice λ\lambdaλ is the post-period sample share n1/(n0+n1)n_1/(n_0+n_1)n1​/(n0​+n1​).

Two implications drive the rest of the section. First, TTT is independent of (D,X)(D,X)(D,X) under PMP_MPM​, because both surveys draw (D,X)(D,X)(D,X) from the same population:

PM(T=1∣D,X)=λ,PM(D=1∣X)=P(D=1∣X).P_M(T=1\mid D,X)=\lambda,\qquad P_M(D=1\mid X)=P(D=1\mid X).PM​(T=1∣D,X)=λ,PM​(D=1∣X)=P(D=1∣X).

So the propensity score can be estimated from the pooled sample, which is used in equations (22) to (30). Second, no individual is seen twice, so Y(1)−Y(0)Y(1)-Y(0)Y(1)−Y(0) is never observed; equation (15) shows how the weight (T−λ)/(λ(1−λ))(T-\lambda)/(\lambda(1-\lambda))(T−λ)/(λ(1−λ)) substitutes for the time difference. The setup requires treatment status DDD to be known in the pre-period sample, and the variable that determines DDD must be excluded from XXX to keep overlap.

Lemma 3.1, equation (9), uses only (Y(1),D,X)(Y(1),D,X)(Y(1),D,X) and (Y(0),D,X)(Y(0),D,X)(Y(0),D,X) separately (it is linear in Y(1)Y(1)Y(1) and Y(0)Y(0)Y(0) and never needs their joint distribution), so it applies:

This is the power series first-step estimator of the propensity score: a linear probability regression of DDD on the first KKK monomials pK(X)p^K(X)pK(X) of the covariates, ordered by total degree (constant, linear terms, squares and interactions, and so on). γ^\widehat{\gamma}γ​ is the OLS coefficient vector, the solution of min⁡γ∑i(Di−pK(Xi)′γ)2\min_\gamma\sum_i(D_i-p^K(X_i)'\gamma)^2minγ​∑i​(Di​−pK(Xi​)′γ)2, and the generalized inverse handles exact collinearity among the monomials (for example, Xj2=XjX_j^2=X_jXj2​=Xj​ for a dummy); the fitted values do not depend on which symmetric generalized inverse is used.
